case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal prisoner may seek habeas corpus relief under 28 U.S.C. 2255(e) — the 'savings clause' — to challenge his firearm conviction based on the Supreme Court's intervening statutory interpretation decision in Rehaif v. United States, when he cannot file a successive Section 2255 motion.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e) (the 'savings clause'), 28 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) (felon in possession of a firearm), 28 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1) (Armed Career Criminal Act), and 28 U.S.C. § 2241 (general federal habeas corpus statute), as interpreted in light of Rehaif v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2191 (2019)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Marcus DeAngelo Jones argues that he should be permitted to challenge his felon-in-possession conviction through a Section 2241 habeas petition via the Section 2255(e) savings clause because the standard Section 2255 motion is 'inadequate or ineffective' to test the legality of his detention. Specifically, Jones contends that after Rehaif — which held that the government must prove a defendant knew of his prohibited status when possessing a firearm — he is actually innocent of the offense as charged, yet he is procedurally barred from raising this claim through a successive Section 2255 motion because Rehaif was a statutory interpretation ruling rather than a new constitutional rule. He argues that denying him access to the savings clause would result in a fundamental miscarriage of justice, leaving him imprisoned for conduct that the Supreme Court has since clarified does not constitute a federal crime under the statute as properly interpreted.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government (represented by Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar) argues that Jones is not entitled to use the Section 2255(e) savings clause to bring a Section 2241 habeas petition because Section 2255 is not 'inadequate or ineffective' merely because Jones is procedurally barred from filing a successive motion. The government contends that the savings clause was intended as a narrow escape valve for structural inadequacies in the Section 2255 remedy itself, not as a workaround for procedural bars that Congress deliberately imposed. The government further argues that allowing prisoners to routinely bypass the gatekeeping requirements of Section 2255 — including the bar on successive petitions based on new statutory interpretation decisions — would undermine the finality interests and limitations Congress carefully built into the federal habeas framework, and that the Eighth Circuit's decision affirming denial of relief should be upheld.

Prost v. Anderson (10th Cir.) — interpreted the savings clause narrowly, focusing on whether Section 2255 was structurally inadequate
In re Davenport (7th Cir.) — broader interpretation of the savings clause allowing its use when a prisoner has no other avenue to raise an intervening statutory interpretation claim
28 U.S.C. § 2255 — the primary federal post-conviction remedy for federal prisoners
28 U.S.C. § 2241 — general habeas corpus statute used when Section 2255 is inadequate
Bousley v. United States, 523 U.S. 614 (1998) — addressed actual innocence in the context of guilty pleas and procedural default
Schlup v. Delo, 513 U.S. 298 (1995) — established the actual innocence gateway standard
McQuiggin v. Perkins, 569 U.S. 383 (2013) — recognized actual innocence as an equitable exception to procedural bars
United States v. Wheeler (4th Cir.) — applied a multi-factor test for savings clause access
Hill v. Masters (6th Cir.) — addressed savings clause availability for sentencing claims

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan's surplusage argument and Justice Jackson's 'illusory opportunity' formulation remain the most serious challenges to my position, and I want to be candid that they have moved me closer to the center — but not across the line. Justice Kagan's cabined reading (requiring both binding circuit precedent foreclosing the claim at the time of the initial motion AND categorical exclusion under § 2255(h)) is genuinely attractive as a limiting principle that would prevent the savings clause from swallowing § 2255(h) entirely, and as Chief Justice I would seriously consider whether a majority opinion could adopt that narrower framework rather than the broader Davenport rule. However, I remain persuaded that even Justice Kagan's cabined reading creates a structural problem: it asks courts to make retrospective judgments about whether circuit precedent was 'binding enough' to render an opportunity 'illusory,' which introduces precisely the kind of unprincipled, case-by-case equitable balancing that AEDPA's architecture was designed to eliminate. The proper institutional response to the genuine hardship Jones faces — and I do not minimize it — is congressional action to extend § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping to meritorious statutory interpretation claims, not judicial expansion of the savings clause that would require us to second-guess Congress's deliberate calibration of finality interests in every successive-petition case going forward.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan's surplusage argument — that a purely structural reading renders the savings clause operative only in vanishingly rare circumstances, violating the canon against surplusage — is the strongest challenge to my position, but it ultimately fails because the savings clause does meaningful work in cases where § 2255 is genuinely unavailable as a structural matter (e.g., where the sentencing court no longer exists or jurisdiction is otherwise absent), without needing to extend to cases where Congress deliberately foreclosed successive petitions. Justice Sotomayor's appeal to actual innocence and fundamental miscarriage of justice is emotionally compelling, but the actual innocence doctrine as articulated in McQuiggin and Bousley operates as an equitable gateway to excuse procedural default — it does not rewrite the statutory text of § 2255(e) to mean something other than what it says, and conflating equitable doctrines with statutory construction is precisely the kind of methodological error that produces unprincipled results. The text of § 2255(e) asks whether the remedy is 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of detention' — and as Justice Gorsuch correctly noted in Prost v. Anderson, a remedy that provided Jones a full and fair opportunity to litigate his claim is not rendered inadequate merely because Congress chose not to extend successive-petition rights to new statutory interpretation decisions; that was a deliberate legislative calibration of finality interests that courts must respect. Allowing the savings clause to swallow § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping would render Congress's carefully constructed AEDPA architecture a nullity, violating the foundational textualist principle that we must give effect to every provision of a statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the most compelling case for the petitioner, arguing that a remedy foreclosed in practice is no remedy at all and that actual innocence principles should override finality concerns. However, their argument conflates two distinct questions: whether § 2255 is structurally adequate as a mechanism, and whether a particular prisoner can obtain a favorable result through it. Congress deliberately excluded new statutory interpretation decisions from § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping provisions — that is not a defect in the remedy, it is the remedy operating exactly as Congress designed it. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, Jones had a full and fair opportunity to raise mens rea arguments in his initial § 2255 motion, and the fact that circuit precedent was unfavorable at the time does not transform a functioning remedy into an inadequate one. Accepting Justice Kagan's surplusage argument would require us to read the savings clause so broadly that it effectively nullifies the successive-petition restrictions Congress enacted in AEDPA — a result that violates the equally important canon against rendering statutory provisions meaningless, since § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping would become a dead letter if prisoners could simply route around it through § 2241 whenever they face an unfavorable statutory interpretation ruling.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest opposing argument — that § 2255(e) addresses structural deficiency in the remedy itself, not a prisoner's procedural eligibility, and that the savings clause 'guarantees process, not results.' But this framing obscures a critical distinction: Jones was not merely procedurally careless or strategic in withholding his claim. At the time of his initial § 2255 motion, binding circuit precedent foreclosed the Rehaif-style argument, and § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping categorically excludes new statutory interpretation decisions regardless of merit. When Congress's own architecture creates a categorical ceiling that prevents any court from ever reaching the merits of a claim that the defendant was convicted of conduct the statute does not criminalize, the remedy is not merely 'unfavorable' — it is genuinely inadequate in any meaningful sense. Justice Kagan correctly identifies that the narrow structural reading renders the savings clause surplusage, since a purely structural deficiency (§ 2255 being unavailable in the relevant district) was already addressed by the 1948 enactment context, and the phrase 'has denied him relief' in § 2255(e) itself contemplates prior use — meaning Congress intended the clause to do additional work beyond mere structural unavailability, work that must include preventing the fundamental miscarriage of justice Jones faces.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's formulation that the savings clause tests the 'structural capacity of the mechanism' rather than 'whether prevailing precedent made success likely' is the most sophisticated version of the respondent position, but it proves too much: under that logic, Congress could make § 2255 nominally available while categorically foreclosing every cognizable claim through binding circuit precedent and § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping, and the savings clause would never be triggered — a reductio ad absurdum that no one on this Court accepts. Justice Gorsuch argues that Congress 'deliberately calibrated' which new developments warrant successive review, but as Justice Jackson correctly responds, Congress did not affirmatively decide that statutory interpretation claims should never receive collateral review; it simply failed to include them in § 2255(h), and reading that silence as a deliberate exclusion ignores that the savings clause exists precisely to address gaps in § 2255's coverage. The narrow reading I've articulated — limiting the savings clause to cases where (1) binding circuit precedent at the time of the initial motion categorically foreclosed the claim, and (2) § 2255(h) independently bars successive review — gives § 2255(h) substantial continuing work while preventing the specific Catch-22 that Justice Jackson identifies, and this cabined construction responds directly to Justice Alito's concern that my reading would swallow AEDPA's gatekeeping architecture. Chief Justice Roberts's suggestion that we might reserve the question for cases involving actual innocence of the underlying conduct is intriguing as a narrowing principle, but Jones's Rehaif claim — that he lacked knowledge of his felon status — is precisely such a claim, so the reservation would not change the outcome here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson's formulation that the savings clause would be 'entirely superfluous' under my reading because § 2255 'always provides some process' is the strongest challenge in this round, but it overstates the case — the savings clause does meaningful work in structural unavailability scenarios that, while rare, are not vanishingly so, and the surplusage canon cannot override the equally weighty canon against reading one provision to swallow another. Justice Kagan's point that the phrase 'such court has denied him relief' presupposes successive use remains the most serious textual challenge, but as I noted previously, this language can be satisfied by cases of genuine structural unavailability following a first motion without extending to cases where Congress deliberately calibrated § 2255(h) to exclude new statutory interpretation decisions. The petitioners' position ultimately requires us to substitute judicial solicitude for congressional judgment about which new legal developments warrant reopening final convictions — precisely the separation of powers concern that animates my textualist methodology. Congress drew a deliberate line between new constitutional rules and new statutory interpretation decisions in § 2255(h), and however uncomfortable the results in individual cases like Jones's, that is a legislative choice courts must respect rather than circumvent through expansive readings of the savings clause.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan's surplusage argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, and Justice Jackson sharpens it by noting that § 2255 always provides *some* process, which would seem to reduce the savings clause to a nullity under the narrow structural reading. However, I continue to believe this overstates the problem: the savings clause does meaningful work in cases where § 2255 is genuinely mechanically unavailable — where the sentencing court no longer exists, where jurisdictional prerequisites cannot be met, or where the remedy was never accessible in the first instance — and these are not as vanishingly rare as Justice Kagan suggests when one considers the full range of federal detention scenarios. The deeper institutional concern that keeps me in the Respondent camp is that Congress in AEDPA made a considered judgment that new statutory interpretation decisions — unlike new constitutional rules — do not warrant reopening final judgments through successive collateral review, and accepting the Davenport framework would effectively allow courts to nullify that legislative calibration whenever a prisoner can characterize a new ruling as a 'statutory clarification.' As Chief Justice Roberts correctly observes, the proper remedy for any structural tension between the savings clause and § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping lies with Congress rather than with judicial rewriting of AEDPA's carefully constructed architecture.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan's sharpest challenge — that the phrase 'has denied him relief' in § 2255(e) affirmatively contemplates successive-petition contexts, meaning Congress intended the savings clause to do work beyond mere structural unavailability — remains the most formidable textual obstacle to my position, and I take it seriously. However, I continue to find it unpersuasive as a basis for the Davenport result: the phrase can be satisfied by successive-petition scenarios involving genuine structural barriers (expired jurisdiction, dissolved courts, limitations periods running through no fault of the prisoner) without also reaching cases where Congress made a deliberate gatekeeping choice in § 2255(h) to exclude new statutory interpretation decisions. Justice Jackson's argument that Jones's 'opportunity' was illusory because binding circuit precedent foreclosed his claim conflates the adequacy of the remedy as a structural mechanism with the favorability of the legal landscape — the savings clause, properly read under its original public meaning, asks whether the prisoner had access to a functioning process, not whether that process was likely to succeed given prevailing precedent, and accepting Jackson's framing would effectively allow courts to nullify § 2255(h)'s deliberate legislative calibration whenever a prisoner can characterize an unfavorable precedential environment as rendering his opportunity 'illusory.' Justice Kagan's proposed limiting principle — requiring both binding foreclosure at the time of the initial motion and categorical exclusion under § 2255(h) — is more cabined than the full Davenport framework, but it still requires courts to make retrospective judgments about whether circuit precedent was sufficiently foreclosing, a line-drawing exercise that will prove unworkable and will gradually erode the finality interests Congress sought to protect in AEDPA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Jones had a 'full and fair opportunity' to raise his mens rea claim remains the respondents' strongest formulation, but it fundamentally misunderstands what 'opportunity' means when binding circuit precedent categorically forecloses a legal theory — an illusory opportunity is not a genuine one, and a remedy that is theoretically available but practically nullified by binding precedent is precisely what 'inadequate or ineffective' must capture. Justice Thomas's response to the surplusage canon — that the savings clause does 'real work' in cases of structural unavailability like a dissolved sentencing court — is clever but ultimately unpersuasive: those scenarios are so vanishingly rare that Congress would not have needed express statutory language to address them, and reading the clause so narrowly reduces it to near-nullity in violation of basic interpretive principles. Justice Gorsuch's separation-of-powers argument that Congress deliberately calibrated which new developments warrant reopening final judgments proves too much — Congress did not affirmatively decide that statutory interpretation claims should never receive collateral review; it simply failed to include them in § 2255(h), and that gap is precisely what the savings clause must fill to prevent the Catch-22 where a prisoner is categorically barred from any court ever reaching the merits of a claim that he was convicted of conduct the statute does not criminalize. My experience as a public defender reinforces that when the entire architecture of post-conviction review systematically forecloses a meritorious innocence claim through no fault of the prisoner, the constitutional guarantee of habeas corpus demands a meaningful pathway, and the savings clause provides it.

John Roberts.reasoning: As a minimalist committed to institutional legitimacy and congressional intent, I find that the savings clause in § 2255(e) cannot be stretched to permit a § 2241 petition merely because procedural bars foreclose a successive § 2255 motion. Congress deliberately constructed the gatekeeping requirements of § 2255(h) to permit successive motions only for new constitutional rules made retroactive by this Court — notably excluding new rules of statutory interpretation — and judicially crafting a third exception would effectively rewrite that legislative judgment, as the Tenth Circuit persuasively reasoned in Prost v. Anderson and the Eleventh Circuit confirmed en banc in McCarthan. While I have genuine sympathy for Jones's position given Rehaif's clarification of the law, the proper remedy for this structural tension lies with Congress, not with courts expanding the savings clause beyond its textual and historical scope. Allowing the savings clause to swallow the carefully calibrated finality framework of § 2255 would undermine the institutional credibility of the federal habeas system and invite a flood of collateral attacks that Congress specifically sought to limit.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e) permits resort to § 2241 only when § 2255 is 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention' — language that, read according to its original public meaning at enactment in 1948, addresses structural deficiencies in the § 2255 remedy itself, not the procedural bars Congress deliberately constructed. Congress enacted the successive-petition gatekeeping requirements with full awareness of the savings clause and chose not to amend it, indicating that these procedural bars were intended to coexist with — not be circumvented by — the savings clause. Allowing Jones to use § 2255(e) as an end-run around the successive-petition bar simply because Rehaif announced a new statutory interpretation would render Congress's carefully calibrated finality provisions a nullity, violating the basic textualist principle that we must give effect to every provision Congress enacted. As I noted in Holder v. Hall, reenactment of statutory language incorporates settled judicial interpretation, and the narrow structural reading of the savings clause — consistent with Prost v. Anderson — best honors the original meaning of 'inadequate or ineffective' as terms of art referring to the mechanism's capacity to function, not a prisoner's procedural eligibility.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I read § 2255(e)'s savings clause narrowly: it permits resort to § 2241 only when § 2255 is structurally 'inadequate or ineffective' as a remedy, not merely when a petitioner is procedurally barred from successive filings by Congress's own deliberate gatekeeping design in AEDPA. Congress specifically limited successive § 2255 motions to new constitutional rules and newly discovered facts — excluding new statutory interpretation decisions like Rehaif — and that was a considered legislative choice about finality that courts should not circumvent through an expansive reading of the savings clause. Allowing Jones to use the savings clause here would effectively nullify the successive-petition restrictions Congress enacted, transforming a narrow escape valve into a broad workaround that swallows the rule. The practical consequences of the broader Davenport-style interpretation are severe: every intervening statutory interpretation decision would become a vehicle for relitigating final convictions, undermining the finality interests and administrative manageability that Congress prioritized in structuring the federal habeas framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The savings clause of 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e) must be interpreted to permit Jones's Section 2241 petition because denying him access to any federal court to vindicate a claim of actual innocence under Rehaif would constitute a fundamental miscarriage of justice. The equitable tradition recognized in McQuiggin v. Perkins and Bousley v. United States establishes that actual innocence serves as a gateway through procedural bars precisely because the imperative of correcting fundamentally unjust incarceration outweighs finality interests — and that principle cannot be cabined by the happenstance that Rehaif was a statutory rather than constitutional ruling. Section 2255 is genuinely 'inadequate or ineffective' here not merely because Jones faces a procedural bar, but because Congress's gatekeeping mechanism for successive petitions under § 2255(h) categorically excludes new statutory interpretation decisions, leaving Jones with no avenue whatsoever to present a claim that he was convicted of conduct the statute — as authoritatively construed by this Court — does not criminalize. The government's narrow reading would effectively immunize from collateral review an entire category of wrongful convictions, trapping prisoners like Jones in a procedural Catch-22 that the savings clause was designed to prevent, and I would adopt a standard requiring access to § 2241 when a prisoner demonstrates actual innocence of a statutory offense based on an intervening Supreme Court decision and has no other procedural avenue for relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) itself contemplates successive use — the phrase 'such court has denied him relief' presupposes a prior § 2255 motion, meaning Congress intended the savings clause to do real work beyond mere structural unavailability. Under a purely narrow reading, the savings clause becomes surplusage, violating the cardinal canon that every statutory provision must have operative effect. When § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping categorically excludes statutory interpretation claims like Rehaif from the successive petition pathway, the remedy is genuinely 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of detention' — not because of a prisoner's procedural failure, but because Congress built a categorical ceiling that forecloses the claim entirely regardless of its merit. Bousley and McQuiggin together establish that actual innocence serves as an equitable gateway to prevent fundamental miscarriages of justice, and a prisoner convicted under a legally erroneous understanding of the statute's elements — where the government never had to prove knowledge of prohibited status — presents precisely the kind of claim that the savings clause must reach to remain coherent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of § 2255(e) asks whether the § 2255 remedy itself is 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of detention' — not whether a particular prisoner has been procedurally barred from using it. As I wrote in Prost v. Anderson, the savings clause 'doesn't guarantee results, only process': a remedy is not inadequate merely because it yields an unfavorable outcome or because a prisoner is now foreclosed from successive use by gatekeeping provisions Congress deliberately enacted. Congress built the successive-petition bar into § 2255 with full awareness that new statutory interpretation decisions — as opposed to new constitutional rules — would not qualify as grounds for successive motions, and that is a considered legislative choice about finality that courts should respect rather than circumvent through an expansive reading of the savings clause. Allowing Rehaif-based claims to flow through § 2241 via the savings clause would effectively nullify the successive-petition framework Congress constructed, substituting judicial solicitude for congressional judgment about the proper balance between finality and error-correction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As an institutionalist who values congressional design and finality, I am persuaded that the savings clause was intended as a narrow structural safety valve rather than a broad workaround for procedural bars Congress deliberately enacted. The AEDPA gatekeeping requirements — including the bar on successive Section 2255 motions based on new statutory interpretation decisions — reflect deliberate congressional choices about finality that courts should respect rather than circumvent through expansive readings of Section 2255(e). While Rehaif represents a significant statutory clarification, allowing prisoners to routinely bypass successive-petition restrictions via the savings clause whenever they cannot satisfy AEDPA's gatekeeping standards would effectively nullify those congressional judgments, undermining the workable framework Congress constructed. The practical institutional concern here is substantial: a broad savings clause interpretation would incentivize prisoners to hold claims in reserve and flood courts with Section 2241 petitions, precisely the outcome Congress sought to prevent through AEDPA's careful architecture, and the Prost v. Anderson approach better honors that legislative design.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying textualist and originalist methodology, the plain language of § 2255(e) requires that the remedy itself be 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention' — not merely that a particular petitioner is procedurally barred from obtaining a favorable result. As Judge Gorsuch articulated in Prost v. Anderson, '[t]he savings clause doesn't guarantee results, only process': Jones had a full and fair opportunity to raise his § 922(g) mens rea arguments through his initial § 2255 motion, and the fact that Congress's deliberately enacted gatekeeping provisions in § 2255(h) now foreclose a successive motion based on Rehaif's statutory interpretation ruling reflects a considered legislative judgment about finality, not a structural deficiency in the § 2255 remedy itself. The Eleventh Circuit's en banc McCarthan decision correctly recognized that adverse circuit precedent or subsequent statutory clarification does not render § 2255 'inadequate or ineffective,' and allowing the savings clause to swallow Congress's carefully constructed AEDPA restrictions would undermine the textual integrity of the entire post-conviction framework. While Rehaif's holding is significant, the proper vehicle for addressing its retroactive application is through Congress or the § 2255(h) gatekeeping process, not through judicial expansion of the savings clause beyond its textual limits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The savings clause's phrase 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention' must be read to encompass situations where a prisoner, through no fault of his own, was procedurally barred from raising a meritorious claim that the Supreme Court subsequently validated through statutory interpretation in Rehaif v. United States. As my background as a public defender makes clear, a remedy that exists only in theory — where circuit precedent foreclosed the claim at the time of the original Section 2255 motion and successive petition rules now bar re-litigation of a statutory interpretation ruling — is not a meaningful remedy at all. The Seventh Circuit's reasoning in In re Davenport is more persuasive than the narrow Prost/McCarthan approach because it recognizes that Congress designed the savings clause as a genuine safety valve against fundamental miscarriages of justice, not merely as a remedy for structural defects in the Section 2255 mechanism itself; denying Jones access to Section 2241 would leave him imprisoned for conduct that the Supreme Court has clarified does not satisfy the statutory elements of the offense as properly construed. This outcome is further supported by the actual innocence principles articulated in Bousley v. United States and McQuiggin v. Perkins, which reflect the Court's longstanding recognition that procedural finality interests must yield when a prisoner presents a credible claim that he was convicted of conduct that does not constitute a federal crime.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito's structural argument — that the savings clause addresses deficiencies in § 2255 as a mechanism rather than individual procedural bars — remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to be precise about why it fails under my minimalist methodology. The key distinction is that when AEDPA's § 2255(h) categorically forecloses an entire class of claims (statutory interpretation decisions that are not 'new rules of constitutional law'), combined with binding circuit precedent that made raising the claim futile at the time of the initial § 2255 motion, the result is not an individual procedural consequence but a systemic gap in the remedial structure — exactly what Justice Kagan identifies as a structural deficiency rather than mere inconvenience. My three-part limiting principle — (1) intervening Supreme Court statutory interpretation establishing an unproven element, (2) claim foreclosed by binding circuit precedent at the time of initial § 2255 motion, and (3) no § 2255(h) gateway available — addresses Justice Thomas's nullification concern by ensuring the savings clause does not swallow AEDPA's finality regime in the ordinary case, while giving the clause substantive content consistent with the anti-surplusage canon that Justice Barrett correctly invokes. As Chief Justice, I will assign the majority opinion with explicit instructions to write narrowly on these three conditions, avoiding any broader language about 'actual innocence' or general equitable principles that could invite the floodgates Justice Alito warns against.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument that the 1948 common law meaning of 'inadequate' — a remedy that cannot provide relief to the same extent as the equitable alternative — actually supports the petitioner deserves serious engagement, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for a reason none of my colleagues have fully addressed: the common law inadequacy of a legal remedy was assessed against the backdrop of the entire legal system's capacity, not against a particular litigant's exhausted opportunities within that system. Jones had a full round of § 2255 review; the remedy was adequate when he used it, and AEDPA's successive petition bar reflects Congress's deliberate judgment that one full round is sufficient. Justice Gorsuch's present-tense 'is' argument remains the most formidable challenge, but as Justice Alito correctly identifies, this reading would transform every § 2255(h) bar into automatic § 2241 eligibility, effectively nullifying AEDPA's gatekeeping provisions that Congress enacted with full awareness of the existing savings clause — and the canon against implied repeal cuts both ways, meaning we should not read § 2255(e) to silently repeal § 2255(h) any more than we should read § 2255(h) to silently repeal § 2255(e). I acknowledge the force of the majority's Suspension Clause concerns, but Boumediene's constitutional floor has never been understood to require that every new statutory interpretation generate a new round of collateral review for federal prisoners who received one full and fair opportunity to challenge their convictions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument that the 1948 common law meaning of 'inadequate' supports Jones because a legal remedy was deemed inadequate when it could not provide equivalent relief deserves serious engagement — but it proves too much, because under that reading any procedural bar that prevents merits review would constitute 'inadequacy,' collapsing the distinction between § 2255(e) and § 2255(h) entirely. Justice Barrett's surplusage concern is the strongest argument against my position, but the savings clause retains genuine work in cases of true structural deficiency — jurisdictional gaps, venue problems, or situations where no court could ever hear the claim — without extending to cases where Congress deliberately erected successive-petition barriers as part of AEDPA's finality regime. The majority's proposed three-part limiting principle, while well-intentioned, lacks any textual anchor in § 2255(e) and will prove unworkable in practice, as courts will struggle to distinguish 'foreclosed by circuit precedent' from ordinary procedural default, inviting the very floodgates problem Congress sought to prevent. I maintain that the proper remedy for Jones's predicament, if any exists, lies with Congress amending § 2255(h) to include new statutory interpretations alongside new constitutional rules — not with this Court rewriting the savings clause to swallow AEDPA's gatekeeping provisions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the strongest opposing argument — that the savings clause addresses only structural deficiencies in § 2255 itself, not procedural bars arising from AEDPA's successive petition restrictions, and that allowing § 2241 access here would nullify Congress's deliberate finality-promoting choices. But this argument proves too much: it treats the savings clause as essentially a dead letter whenever AEDPA applies, which cannot be what Congress intended when it left § 2255(e) intact after enacting AEDPA in 1996. As Justice Kagan correctly observes, § 2255(h)'s gatekeeping provisions were enacted 48 years after the savings clause and do not purport to modify it — reading the later provision to swallow the earlier one violates basic canons of statutory construction. Most critically, when Rehaif established that the government must prove an element it never proved at Jones's trial, and when circuit precedent foreclosed raising that argument at the time of his initial § 2255 motion, the structural operation of § 2255 combined with AEDPA's successive petition bar creates exactly the kind of genuine inadequacy — not mere inconvenience — that the savings clause was designed to address, because Jones has never had any meaningful opportunity to litigate whether his conduct was actually criminal under a correct reading of the statute.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito's structural distinction — that § 2255(e) asks whether the § 2255 mechanism itself is inadequate, not whether a particular prisoner's litigation history has exhausted his access — remains the most serious challenge to my position, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for a reason Justice Jackson articulates well: when AEDPA's successive petition bar categorically forecloses an entire class of claims (Rehaif-based statutory interpretation challenges) from merits review, that categorical foreclosure is a structural deficiency in the § 2255 system as applied to that class, not merely an individual procedural consequence. Justice Thomas argues that Congress enacted AEDPA against the backdrop of the savings clause and chose not to modify it, inferring that Congress understood the savings clause would not undermine the new gatekeeping provisions — but this inference cuts both ways: Congress also chose not to repeal or narrow § 2255(e), and implied repeal is disfavored. I am persuaded by Justice Roberts's three-part limiting principle — requiring an intervening Supreme Court statutory interpretation, foreclosure by binding circuit precedent at the time of the initial § 2255 motion, and no alternative § 2255(h) gateway — as the appropriate cabining mechanism that preserves AEDPA's finality interests in the vast majority of cases while giving the savings clause genuine substantive content rather than rendering it surplusage.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito's structural argument — that § 2255(e) asks whether the mechanism itself is deficient, not whether a particular prisoner's litigation history has exhausted his access — remains the most serious challenge to my position, but it ultimately fails on its own textualist terms. The savings clause asks whether § 2255 'is inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention' — the possessive 'his' is doing real work, directing the inquiry to this prisoner's actual remedial capacity, not to the mechanism in the abstract. Justice Thomas's originalist point about 1948 meaning, which Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson both engage, actually reinforces this: at common law, a remedy was inadequate when it could not provide equivalent relief, and a § 2255 system that categorically cannot reach the merits of a Rehaif claim — because § 2255(h) limits successive petitions to new constitutional rules, not new statutory interpretations — is inadequate in precisely that classical sense. I remain persuaded by the three-part limiting principle I articulated in Round 1, which addresses Justice Alito's nullification concern by ensuring the savings clause is triggered only when circuit precedent foreclosed the claim at the time of the initial motion, the intervening decision announces a new statutory interpretation, and the error goes to whether the conduct was ever criminal — this cabined rule preserves AEDPA's finality regime in the vast majority of cases while preventing the savings clause from becoming a constitutional nullity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito's structural argument — that the savings clause addresses deficiencies in § 2255 as a mechanism rather than individual procedural bars — remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to be precise about why it ultimately fails. The distinction between 'structural' and 'individual procedural' inadequacy collapses in Jones's case because the successive petition bar categorically forecloses an entire class of claims — those resting on new statutory interpretations rather than new constitutional rules — meaning no prisoner in Jones's position can ever obtain merits review through § 2255, which is a systemic gap, not merely an individual misfortune. Justice Kagan's point about the 1948 common law meaning of 'inadequate' is persuasive: a legal remedy was inadequate when it could not provide relief to the same extent as the equitable alternative, and § 2255 plainly cannot reach Rehaif claims for prisoners like Jones. I remain committed to Justice Barrett's and Justice Roberts's instinct to cabin this ruling narrowly — requiring (1) an intervening Supreme Court statutory interpretation, (2) foreclosure by binding circuit precedent at the time of the initial § 2255 motion, and (3) categorical unavailability under § 2255(h) — because this limiting principle preserves AEDPA's finality regime in the vast majority of cases while honoring the savings clause as something more than surplusage.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito's structural argument — that the savings clause addresses deficiencies in § 2255 as a mechanism rather than individual procedural bars — remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage it with full rigor. The distinction he draws between structural inadequacy and individual procedural foreclosure is analytically coherent, but it breaks down precisely in cases like this one: when AEDPA's § 2255(h) categorically forecloses an entire class of claims (those resting on new statutory interpretations rather than new constitutional rules), the result is not an individual procedural bar but a systemic gap in the § 2255 mechanism itself — which is structural inadequacy in the ordinary sense of that term. Justice Thomas's originalist point about the 1948 meaning of 'inadequate' actually reinforces this conclusion, as Justice Kagan correctly observes: at common law, a legal remedy was inadequate when it could not provide relief to the same extent as the equitable alternative, and § 2255 categorically cannot reach Rehaif-based statutory claims through any available gateway. I remain persuaded that the savings clause must be given substantive content, but I continue to insist — consistent with my prior reasoning and Justice Roberts's minimalist instincts — that any holding be cabined to require (1) an intervening Supreme Court statutory interpretation establishing a new element, (2) genuine foreclosure by binding circuit precedent at the time of the initial § 2255 motion, and (3) categorical unavailability of any § 2255(h) gateway, thereby preserving AEDPA's finality regime in the vast majority of cases.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito's most refined argument — that § 2255(e)'s savings clause asks whether the § 2255 remedy as a structural mechanism is inadequate, not whether a particular prisoner's litigation history has exhausted his access — remains the strongest counterargument, but it ultimately fails to account for the categorical nature of the bar Jones faces. As Justice Kagan correctly identifies, when Rehaif's statutory interpretation does not qualify as a 'new rule of constitutional law' under § 2255(h)(2), the successive petition bar is not a consequence of Jones's individual litigation choices but rather a structural gap in the § 2255 mechanism itself — no prisoner in Jones's class can obtain merits review through § 2255, which is precisely the kind of systemic inadequacy the savings clause was designed to address. Justice Thomas's argument that Congress enacted AEDPA against the backdrop of the savings clause and chose not to modify it actually cuts both ways: Congress also chose not to modify § 2255(e) to exclude cases like Jones's, and the most natural reading of leaving both provisions intact is that they operate independently rather than that the later provision silently swallows the earlier one. I am further persuaded by Justice Roberts's cabined three-condition framework — intervening Supreme Court statutory interpretation establishing an unproven element, foreclosure by binding circuit precedent at the time of initial § 2255 motion, and no § 2255(h) gateway — which addresses the floodgates concern without rendering the savings clause a dead letter, and which my background as a public defender confirms is essential to prevent permanent imprisonment for conduct that authoritative interpretation reveals was never criminal.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of Section 2255(e) employs a present-tense inquiry — whether the Section 2255 remedy 'is' inadequate or ineffective — which means the relevant question is whether Jones can currently obtain meaningful review of a potentially invalid conviction, not whether he theoretically could have raised the Rehaif argument at some prior point. When AEDPA's successive petition bar forecloses a prisoner from vindicating a substantive statutory interpretation ruling that may render his conduct non-criminal, Section 2255 is genuinely 'inadequate or ineffective' in the most literal sense, and the savings clause must function as a true safety valve rather than a dead letter. My preference for narrow rulings counsels against endorsing any broad circuit test like Prost that categorically forecloses savings clause access whenever a claim was theoretically 'available' under prior law, as that reading raises serious Suspension Clause concerns under Boumediene and risks the Court's institutional legitimacy by tolerating continued imprisonment for potentially non-criminal conduct. I would resolve this case on the narrow ground that Rehaif's new statutory construction — establishing an element the government never proved — is precisely the category of substantive legal error the savings clause was designed to reach, without broadly resolving every circuit split over the clause's full scope.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must examine what 'inadequate or ineffective' meant when Congress enacted § 2255(e) in 1948. The text of the savings clause is a narrow exception, not a broad escape hatch, and the mere fact that AEDPA's successive petition restrictions bar Jones's claim does not render § 2255 'inadequate or ineffective' — it renders it unavailable due to his own prior litigation choices, which is a fundamentally different condition. Congress deliberately enacted AEDPA's gatekeeping provisions to bring finality to criminal judgments, and allowing prisoners to routinely circumvent those restrictions via § 2241 would nullify congressional intent as expressed in the statutory text. While I acknowledge the research suggesting Congress left the savings clause untouched after AEDPA, the proper reading consistent with original public meaning is that the clause preserves the writ only in structural circumstances where § 2255 categorically cannot reach a claim — not merely where a prisoner is procedurally foreclosed due to successive petition rules he could have anticipated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e) makes the savings clause available only when the Section 2255 remedy 'is inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention' — not merely when a particular prisoner is procedurally barred from using it due to AEDPA's successive petition restrictions. Allowing Jones to invoke Section 2241 simply because AEDPA's gatekeeping provisions foreclose a successive Section 2255 motion would effectively nullify Congress's deliberate restrictions on successive petitions, as the Tenth Circuit correctly recognized in Prost v. Anderson. The savings clause was designed to address structural deficiencies in the Section 2255 remedy itself — situations where the mechanism categorically cannot provide relief — not to serve as an end-run around AEDPA's finality-promoting restrictions whenever a prisoner is individually barred from filing again. Furthermore, Rehaif announced a statutory interpretation rule, not a constitutional one, and permitting routine circumvention of AEDPA's successive petition bar via Section 2241 for statutory claims would undermine the congressional judgment that finality interests in criminal judgments must be respected after one full round of collateral review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The savings clause of § 2255(e) must be interpreted to permit habeas relief under § 2241 when a prisoner faces a potentially invalid conviction based on a subsequent Supreme Court statutory interpretation ruling like Rehaif v. United States, because the Prost and McCarthan standards conflate procedural unavailability with structural inadequacy in a manner that produces unjust results for vulnerable incarcerated individuals. When Congress enacted the savings clause, it recognized that § 2255 could become genuinely inadequate — not merely inconvenient — and Rehaif's holding that the government must prove a defendant knew of his prohibited status represents a fundamental change in what the statute actually requires, meaning Jones may be imprisoned for conduct that was never actually criminal under a proper reading of § 922(g)(1). The Fourth Circuit's Wheeler standard more faithfully honors both the text and purpose of the savings clause by asking whether the structural operation of § 2255 — including AEDPA's successive petition bar — prevents meaningful review of a claim that could not have been raised earlier, rather than asking only whether the prisoner theoretically could have argued a foreclosed position. Allowing the Prost/McCarthan approach to stand would mean that prisoners like Jones, who bear no fault for failing to anticipate a Supreme Court ruling that postdated their initial § 2255 motion, are permanently foreclosed from challenging convictions that may rest on a legally insufficient basis, a result that offends fundamental principles of fairness and the constitutional guarantee of habeas corpus recognized in Boumediene v. Bush.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) preserves habeas access whenever the § 2255 remedy is 'inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of detention,' and that language must be given its natural meaning independent of § 2255(h)'s successive-petition gatekeeping, which was enacted nearly 50 years later and does not purport to modify the savings clause. When Rehaif established that the government must prove a defendant knew of his prohibited status — a statutory interpretation that was foreclosed by circuit precedent at the time of Jones's initial § 2255 motion — he never had a meaningful opportunity to litigate a claim that goes to the core legality of his conviction, precisely the circumstance the savings clause was designed to address. Allowing § 2255(h)'s procedural bar to swallow § 2255(e)'s substantive guarantee would produce the incoherent result that Congress simultaneously preserved habeas review of fundamental legality claims while categorically eliminating it whenever a prisoner has already filed once, a reading that neither the text nor the legislative history supports. A pragmatic, workable construction requires that the savings clause remain available for claims — like a Rehaif challenge — that could not have been raised or adjudicated on the merits through the ordinary § 2255 process, consistent with the reasoning in In re Davenport and the Fourth Circuit's approach in Wheeler.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of § 2255(e) asks whether the remedy 'is' — present tense — inadequate or ineffective, not whether it ever was available in the past. When AEDPA's successive-petition bar categorically forecloses a prisoner from raising a claim based on an intervening statutory interpretation like Rehaif, § 2255 is, at that moment, genuinely inadequate to test the legality of detention — not merely inconvenient or procedurally barred through the prisoner's own fault. My textualist methodology requires giving effect to the word 'inadequate' according to its ordinary meaning: a remedy that cannot, as a structural matter, provide any relief is inadequate, full stop. Furthermore, permitting the government to imprison someone for conduct that a subsequent authoritative statutory interpretation reveals was never criminal raises serious constitutional concerns under the Suspension Clause and separation of powers — courts, not procedural default rules, must retain the power to say what the law is and release those held unlawfully, consistent with Boumediene's recognition of habeas corpus as a constitutional floor.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of Section 2255(e) employs a present-tense inquiry — whether Section 2255 'is' inadequate or ineffective — which means the relevant question is whether Jones can currently obtain relief through Section 2255, not whether he theoretically could have raised the claim earlier. Because AEDPA's successive petition restrictions under Section 2255(h) bar Jones from filing another Section 2255 motion based on Rehaif's statutory interpretation ruling (which does not qualify as a 'new rule of constitutional law' under 2255(h)(2)), Section 2255 is presently inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention, triggering the savings clause. History and tradition counsel that habeas corpus has always served as a fundamental check on unlawful imprisonment, and allowing someone to remain incarcerated for conduct that Rehaif clarified was never criminal raises serious Suspension Clause concerns that counsel against the government's narrow reading. While I share the government's concern about finality and AEDPA's structural integrity, the savings clause was preserved by Congress precisely as a safety valve for circumstances like these, and reading it to be a nullity whenever AEDPA's successive petition bar applies would render the provision meaningless.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A careful textualist reading of § 2255(e)'s 'inadequate or ineffective' language, understood against its 1948 backdrop and the traditional equity principle that a remedy is inadequate when it cannot provide relief to the same extent as the alternative, suggests that § 2255 is genuinely inadequate — not merely procedurally inconvenient — when AEDPA's successive-petition bar categorically forecloses a prisoner from presenting a claim based on an intervening statutory interpretation like Rehaif. The savings clause is a substantive safety valve, not mere surplusage, and reading it to mean only that the initial filing opportunity existed — regardless of whether the claim could ever receive merits review — would render the clause largely meaningless in violation of basic textual canons. However, I am mindful of the government's serious concern that permitting Rehaif-based § 2241 claims would effectively nullify AEDPA's finality-promoting restrictions on successive petitions, and I would cabin any ruling narrowly to require a showing of actual, concrete remedial inadequacy — not merely adverse circuit precedent — consistent with the Davenport framework's requirement that the structural defect, not mere procedural bar, be the source of inadequacy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The savings clause of § 2255(e) must be read to permit habeas relief under § 2241 when a prisoner faces a genuine risk of incarceration for conduct that the Supreme Court has subsequently clarified is not criminal — here, Rehaif v. United States established that the government must prove the defendant knew of his prohibited status, an element that was not required at Jones's trial and could not meaningfully have been raised in his initial § 2255 motion under then-prevailing circuit law. The Prost standard's narrow construction — treating § 2255 as adequate merely because a claim was theoretically raisable even when foreclosed by binding precedent — conflates procedural availability with genuine adequacy, a distinction the savings clause's text and history demand we honor. As the Second and Third Circuits recognized in Triestman and Dorsainvil, denying any avenue of collateral review to a prisoner who may be legally innocent under a correct statutory interpretation raises serious Suspension Clause concerns under Boumediene, and Congress, legislating against the backdrop of Sanders, did not intend AEDPA's successive petition restrictions to swallow the savings clause entirely. My background as a public defender reinforces that procedural finality cannot be an absolute trump when the underlying conviction may rest on a legally deficient foundation — the writ of habeas corpus exists precisely for such circumstances.
